signals.excerpt:
- New compute service: Agent Compute Engine is a purpose-built compute service providing high-performance, hardware-isolated microVM sandboxes alongside expanded agent governance capabilities like Agent Gateway and Agent Registry, all in the service of securing and scaling autonomous AI agents. Its primary benefits include rapid sub-second activation, extreme workload density through copy-on-write memory sharing, enterprise-grade security and identity management, and cross-cloud observability.
- AI Hypercomputer updates: At NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 we announced updates to our agentic infrastructure, including to A5X instances powered by the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, Virgo Network scale-out fabric, and Managed Lustre storage. These co-engineered advancements provide enterprises with accelerated performance, enhanced sovereign AI controls, while advanced Confidential Computing capabilities help you train and deploy complex multi-step models securely and efficiently.
- GKE product update: CPU startup boost for GKE, in preview, uses Kubernetes In-place Pod Resize to dynamically elevate container CPU resources during initialization and scale them back down to steady-state levels without having to restart the containers. This feature removes startup throttling and accelerates cold starts by up to 2x for demanding workloads, helping to lower cloud infrastructure costs.
- GKE product update: The preview of the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) brings low-touch deployment, automated lifecycle management, enterprise credential security, and fleet-wide governance to Wiz's eBPF runtime threat detection for both Standard and Autopilot GKE clusters.
- Modernization tools: Together at last. Google Cloud Modernize brings Google Cloud’s migration and modernization tools, including Migration Center, Google Cloud VMware Engine, Google Cloud Mainframe Modernization and our new EKS-to-GKE Migration Agent, into a single portfolio. Enterprise teams now have purpose-built agentic capabilities across infrastructure assessment, platform modernization, and application modernization.
- Cloud Run product update: Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run automatically scale worker pools based on Temporal task queue demands and scale down to zero when idle. This integration eliminates cluster management, lowers costs, using Temporal Worker Versioning to safely handle stateful, long-running workflows and AI agent workloads.
- New open-source product: llm-d 1.0 is an open-source, Kubernetes-native serving stack that turns a cluster of model servers into a coordinated serving pool, unifying distributed LLM inference across mixed Google Cloud TPU and GPU fleets. Co-founded by Google and partners, it provides production-ready benefits such as cache-aware routing, tiered KV cache offloading, and priority-based flow control to dramatically improve context reuse, reduce time-to-first-token latency, and efficiently scale multi-tenant agent workloads.
- New open-source product: Working with Meta, we open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch stack that integrates Google TPUs directly into the PyTorch ecosystem alongside GPUs and CPUs. Now developers can train, serve, and deploy models natively on TPUs using familiar frameworks like Hugging Face, vLLM, and TorchTitan.
- Google Distributed Cloud updates: Organizations that operate under strict sovereignty mandates would love to use AI to help them process data, but can’t send it to the cloud. The latest version of Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) air-gapped brings frontier AI models and multimodal enterprise search with Gemini into these isolated environments. In addition, GDC air-gapped supports NVIDIA HGX B300 systems based on the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra architecture, and features enhanced networking and security capabilities. 
- Edge inference product: Google open-sourced ML Drift, a cross-platform on-device GPU compute engine built for LiteRT that abstracts hardware complexities across OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal, and WebGPU. The framework delivers peak performance, enhanced 5D tensor support, and memory efficiency for both classical machine learning workloads and advanced generative AI models at the edge.
- Open-weight model support: Reflection's Beam is an open-weight, 501-parameter model released under an Apache 2.0 license designed specifically for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. signals.title: Shipping an Agentic RAG Assistant on AWS Lambda with LangGraph and Terraform - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Shipping an Agentic RAG Assistant on AWS Lambda with LangGraph and Terraform - DEV Community
Ved Suthar
Posted on Oct 30
# Shipping an Agentic RAG Assistant on AWS Lambda with LangGraph and Terraform
*How I built a tool-calling ReAct agent over a private knowledge base, packaged it as a Lambda container, and provisioned all of it as code.*
Most retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) demos follow one fixed path: embed the question, fetch the top-k chunks, put them in a prompt, and return whatever the model says. That works until a question needs more than one lookup, or needs arithmetic the model shouldn't guess at, or doesn't need retrieval at all.
I wanted an assistant that could decide what to do: search the knowledge base, search again with a better query, call a calculator, or just answer. I also wanted to deploy it with no hand-configured infrastructure. This post walks through the design: a LangGraph ReAct agent, FAISS for vector search, a FastAPI interface, a provider-agnostic LLM layer, and an AWS Lambda container image provisioned end-to-end with Terraform.
## Why "agentic" RAG?
In classic RAG, retrieval is a step that always runs once. In agentic RAG, retrieval is a **tool**. The model works in a loop (the ReAct pattern: reason, act, observe) and picks which tool to call based on what it has learned so far.
That gets you three things:
1. **Multi-hop questions.** If the first search returns half the answer, the agent can write a sharper second query.
2. **Exact computation.** "What's the combined budget of projects A and B?" should go to a calculator, not to next-token prediction.
3. **Skipping retrieval.** A greeting or a follow-up about the previous answer doesn't need a vector search.
The cost is more LLM calls per question and a bit of extra complexity. LangGraph keeps that complexity manageable.
## Architecture at a glance
```
Client ──HTTPS──▶ Lambda (container image)
                     │
                     ├─ FastAPI app (via ASGI adapter)
                     │
                     └─ LangGraph agent
                          ├─ LLM node (OpenAI or Anthropic)
                          └─ Tool node
                               ├─ retriever → FAISS index
                               └─ calculator
```
I split the codebase into small modules so each part could be tested on its own:
* `config` holds typed settings (model provider, model name, top-k, index path), loaded from environment variables.
* `retriever` loads the FAISS index and returns ranked chunks with their source metadata.
* `tools` defines the retriever and calculator as tools the LLM can call.
* `llm` is a thin, provider-agnostic wrapper.
* `graph` wires the agent.
* `api` is the FastAPI layer.
## The agent graph
LangGraph models an agent as a state machine. The state is mainly the list of messages; nodes read the state and add to it; edges decide what runs next.
The ReAct loop needs two nodes and one conditional edge:
```
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START, END
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode

...

graph = StateGraph(MessagesState)
graph.add_node("agent", call_model)
graph.add_node("tools", ToolNode(tools))
graph.add_edge(START, "agent")
graph.add_conditional_edges("agent", should_continue, ["tools", END])
graph.add_edge("tools", "agent")
app_graph = graph.compile()
```
The model either asks for tool calls or produces a final answer. If it asks for tools, `ToolNode` runs them, appends the results as tool messages, and control goes back to the model. I also set a recursion limit when invoking the graph so a confused model can't loop forever.
Writing the loop as an explicit graph, rather than hiding it inside an agent class, paid off quickly. I could see every transition, test `should\_continue` with plain unit tests, and add nodes later (a query-rewriting step, for example) without touching the rest.
## Tools: retriever and calculator
The retriever tool's docstring matters as much as its code, because the model reads it to decide when to call it:
```
@tool
def retrieve_docs(query: str) -> str:
    """Search the private knowledge base. Use for any question about
    internal documents. Returns the most relevant passages with sources."""
    hits = retriever.search(query, k=settings.top_k)
    return "\n\n".join(f"[{h.source}] {h.text}" for h in hits)
```
Returning the source with each passage lets the model cite where an answer came from, and makes bad retrievals easy to spot while debugging.
The calculator is deliberately narrow. It evaluates arithmetic expressions with a small safe parser rather than Python's `eval`, because tool inputs are model-generated text and should be treated as untrusted.
## FAISS: simple, local, fast to load
For a private knowledge base of modest size, FAISS is a good fit: no separate database to run, and the index is just a file. I build the index offline (chunk documents, embed them, write the index plus a metadata file mapping vector IDs to text and source), then ship it with the application.
On Lambda that has a nice property: the index loads from the container's filesystem at cold start and stays in memory for warm invocations. I load it once at module level, not per request, so warm requests skip that cost.
The trade-off is that updating the knowledge base means rebuilding the index and redeploying. For a knowledge base that changes rarely, I'll take that over running a vector database.
## A provider-agnostic LLM layer
I didn't want the agent tied to one vendor. The `llm` module exposes one factory that returns a chat model supporting tool binding, chosen by config:
```
def get_llm(settings: Settings):
    if settings.provider == "openai":
        return ChatOpenAI(model=settings.model, temperature=0)
    if settings.provider == "anthropic":
        return ChatAnthropic(model=settings.model, temperature=0)
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown provider: {settings.provider}")
```
The rest of the code depends only on this interface. Switching providers is a config change, which also makes it easy to compare how different models behave with the same tools and prompts. API keys come from the environment and never live in the code or the image.
## FastAPI on Lambda
FastAPI gives a typed request and response schema and automatic docs during local development. To run the same app on Lambda, I wrap it with an ASGI-to-Lambda adapter such as Mangum, so one codebase serves both `uvicorn` locally and Lambda in production.
```

signals.title: Three MoE Inference Optimizations NVIDIA Measured on DGX Spark - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
* The DGX Spark is a compact AI computer from NVIDIA for developers and researchers, built on the GB10 Grace Blackwell superchip with up to 128 GB of unified memory, and the model benchmarked on it here is Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI, a mixture-of-experts model with 124 billion parameters.
* NVIDIA's post published on 27 October 2026 measures three changes to that model's decode loop at batch size 1, and reports time per output token falling from 27.71 ms to 9.72 ms.
* Profiling showed decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time, and the MoE computation plus the output projection dominated it.
* Humming MXFP4 kernels compile at run time for the model's real shapes, which measured +9.3% decode throughput.
* Online FP8 quantization halves the LM head weight reads and brings the stack to +21.7% over baseline.
* Multi-token prediction with NEXTN turns one verification into four tokens, and the synthetic workload accepted 3.90 tokens per round.
* GSM8K measured a 42.5% throughput gain across 1,319 questions with accuracy unchanged within 0.08 of a point.
* The synthetic workload overstates the gain a real workload sees, because repetitive output is easier to draft.
* One missing interface makes the stack slower than baseline, which is why the vendor recommends validating each optimization at startup.
Official NVIDIA product photo of the DGX Spark family, from the product page at nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark, retrieved 29 October 2026.
A batch of one is the least glamorous benchmark in AI infrastructure and the one most people actually run. It is the shape of a coding assistant answering one developer, a document summariser serving one request, an agent waiting on its own next token. NVIDIA chose that shape for this measurement, and the result is a useful case study in how much of a decode step is spent reading weights off memory.
## Decoding was memory-bound on a 124-billion-parameter model at batch size 1
Ling-3.0-flash keeps 5.1 billion of its 124 billion parameters active per token. It has 42 layers, 35 of them Kimi Delta Attention linear-attention layers and seven multi-head latent attention layers, and each MoE layer routes a token to eight of 512 routed experts alongside one shared expert. The LM head projects a hidden dimension of 2,560 onto a vocabulary of 157,184 tokens.
Capture of the NVIDIA technical blog post carrying the measurement, developer.nvidia.com/blog/3-ways-to-boost-moe-inference-on-nvidia-dgx-spark, taken 29 October 2026.
At batch size 1, arithmetic units sit idle and the decode step waits on memory bandwidth. Two operations carried the cost: the routed-expert computation, and the vocabulary projection whose entire weight block has to be read for every generated token. NVIDIA's three optimizations attack those two costs in two different ways, and the article's value is that it reports each one separately before stacking them.
## Humming MXFP4 kernels compile at run time for the model's real shapes
The baseline ran the official W4A8 recipe: FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, CUTLASS dense GEMM, and the `--enable-fp32-lm-head` option. Swapping the MoE backend for Humming moved time per output token from 27.71 ms to 25.35 ms and decode throughput from 36.09 to 39.45 tokens per second, a 9.3% gain.
The mechanism explains the modest size of the gain. Humming uses NVRTC to generate and compile CUBINs at run time for the actual M, N and K dimensions, the data types and the GPU architecture, then caches them in `\~/.humming/cache`.

...

Netics editorial visual built from the post's end-to-end table: baseline against all three optimizations across all 1,319 GSM8K test questions.
## Online FP8 quantization halves the LM head weight reads
The checkpoint stores the LM head in BF16 and ... Its vocabulary GEMM is 157,184 by 2,560, and every generated token reads that whole block. Under a bandwidth bottleneck it is the obvious target.
NVIDIA applies a dynamic FP8 quantization configuration when the LM head is constructed, leaving the rest of the model on the checkpoint's FP8 and MXFP4 settings. That halves the read volume for the layer, and the setting is one environment variable, `SGLANG\_ENABLE\_FP8\_LM\_HEAD=1`.

...

Netics editorial visual: the order the three techniques apply to a decode loop, and the startup check that confirms each one is active.
## Multi-token prediction turns each verification into four tokens
The first two optimizations reduce the cost of a decode step.

...

The configuration uses three draft steps and a four-token verification window: the draft predicts three tokens in sequence, and the target verifies four positions at once, accepting the correct prefix. The benefit depends on accept length and on the verification-cost ratio, which measured about 2.26. The interesting part of the analysis is where that cost came from. At batch size 1, small KV reads and larger weight reads made expert activation the principal verification cost: a normal decode activates eight experts for one token while verification over four tokens can activate up to 32.
On the synthetic 32K-input, 2K-output workload the stack reached 9.72 ms and 102.88 tokens per second, 185.1% over baseline, with an accept length of 3.90. That number is where a careful reader slows down.
Netics editorial visual: the four figures that decide whether this stack is worth deploying, each traceable to the post's tables.
## GSM8K measured a 42.5% throughput gain across 1,319 questions
The second evaluation is the one worth trusting more. NVIDIA ran all 1,319 GSM8K test questions with five-shot prompting, temperature 0.6, top\_p 0.95, top\_k 29, a 32,768-token ceiling and chain-of-thought enabled, holding sampling, parser, seed and memory allocation fixed.
Across that set, time per output token went from 26.45 ms to 18.56 ms, decode throughput from 37.81 to 53.89 tokens per second, a 42.5% gain, and mean latency from 15.21 s to 11.49 s. P50 fell from 8.36 s to 6.11 s and P95 from 50.20 s to 38.60 s. GSM8K accuracy moved from 96.89% to 96.82%, and the run recorded zero errors and zero truncations. The measured gain is real and roughly a quarter of the synthetic claim.
## The synthetic workload overstates the gain a real workload sees
NVIDIA states the caveat itself, which is rarer than it should be. Accept length was 3.90 on the synthetic run against 2.68 on GSM8K. Three differences explain most of the gap: synthetic output repeats, which makes drafting easy; the synthetic test decoded greedily while the real evaluation sampled at temperature 0.6 with top\_p 0.95 and top\_k 29; and the synthetic workload fixed output at 2K tokens while the median GSM8K output is about 310 tokens, which spreads the fixed overhead reductions over a much shorter generation.
Capture of the DGX Spark user guide landing page, docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgx-spark/index.html, taken 29 October 2026.
That last point is the one to carry into a deployment decision. Speculative decoding pays per token generated, and the two other optimizations pay per step, so a workload with short answers collects most of the first two gains and a fraction of the third. The same discipline applies to any vendor benchmark: the useful question is which of the measured mechanisms your own traffic can reach. A previous analysis of how CUDA 13.4 turns a GPU fraction into an enforceable memory limit followed the same logic, because a capability only counts once the platform enforces it under your workload.
## One missing interface makes the stack slower than baseline
Stacking the three optimizations is where the article earns its keep. Each worked alone. Together, the FP8 LM-head path and MTP need the draft model to share the entire LM-head module, because the draft has to interpret the same quantized weights as the target. The original Ling NEXTN implementation exposed only the weight tensor.
Netics editorial visual: the integration requirement behind the FP8 LM head and MTP pairing, and the failure mode when the interface is absent.
Without the interface the framework falls back silently: the draft receives FP8 weights and reads them as BF16, accept length collapses to 1.00, and throughput ends up below the configuration with no optimizations at all. Nothing fails, nothing logs an error, and the only symptom is that the machine is slower than it was before someone made it faster. NVIDIA's guidance is to validate at startup that every optimization is active, which is more reliable than inferring configuration state from a later performance number.
This paragraph belongs in an internal wiki. A silent fallback in an inference stack can create a capacity incident on launch day, so startup validation belongs in the deployment checklist. The model, the kernels and the quantization are NVIDIA's engineering; the discipline of proving each layer is active belongs to whoever operates the deployment. Related resources include Netics, and the deployment planning page.
*Originally published on the Netics blog.*

# LongCat- 2.5 Native Multimodality for Agentic Tasks

2026-11-1

We introduce LongCat-2.5, a native multimodal model for long-horizon agentic tasks. With 1.6 trillion total parameters and approximately 48 billion activated per token, it builds on LongCat-2.0 with stronger native visual understanding and agentic coding.

We incorporate more long-horizon trajectories into long-sequence training and use large-scale long-horizon reinforcement learning to strengthen end-to-end engineering capabilities across complex codebase development and full-project builds. We continue to scale this training pipeline through data synthesis, environment construction, and mixed training across harnesses. We also convert real-world agent failure trajectories into reproducible, verifiable training tasks, continually adding targeted training data to address model capability gaps.

LongCat-2.5 also represents visual signals as multi-level discrete tokens, enabling the backbone to process visual and textual inputs in a unified token-based format. Combining native visual understanding with agentic coding delivers strong visual coding performance, while also supporting creative design and 3D tasks.

These advances are supported by continued infrastructure improvements. We optimize long-context training and W4A4 inference on domestic AI accelerators, while numerical consistency between training and inference and long-context rollout optimizations enable efficient large-scale long-horizon RL.

signals.title: Sub-Millisecond RAG Faithfulness Evaluation with agentic-rag-faithfulness - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Posted on Oct 31 

# Sub-Millisecond RAG Faithfulness Evaluation with agentic-rag-faithfulness 

Evaluating whether a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system actually sticks to retrieved context usually requires calling an expensive LLM judge (like GPT-4), adding hundreds of milliseconds of latency and recurring API costs.

agentic-rag-faithfulness is an ultra-fast, local evaluation library that calculates RAG faithfulness scores in under 1 millisecond with support for both English and Arabic text.

# Agentic RAG Faithfulness Evaluator 🎯🧠

 

A lightweight, sub-millisecond evaluation library to measure RAG faithfulness and detect LLM hallucinations against retrieved context documents in Arabic and English.

Developed by Tarek Mohamed (@seotarek)

## ⚡ Why Local & Sub-Millisecond? 

- Real-Time Guardrails: Can be run directly inside production serving pipelines before streaming answers to end users.
- Zero API Costs: No external LLM judge tokens required for evaluation.
- Cross-Lingual Support: Specifically calibrated for complex Arabic morphology as well as standard English text.

## 💻 Quick Code Example 

```
from rag_faithfulness import FaithfulnessEvaluator

evaluator = FaithfulnessEvaluator()

context = "Valorex is an ultra-fast native desktop browser built in Rust."
response = "Valorex is written in Python and uses Electron."

score = evaluator.evaluate(context=context, response=response)
print(f"Faithfulness Score: {score.score:.2f} (Hallucination Detected: {score.is_hallucination})")
# Output: Faithfulness Score: 0.12 (Hallucination Detected: True)

signals.title: MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Now Live on Tenstorrent
signals.excerpt:
# MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Now Live on Tenstorrent

 November 2, 2026 - 

Tenstorrent is now serving MiniMax M3.1 Flash on Cloud, with both prefill and decode running on Tenstorrent Galaxy®. 

MiniMax released the open weights for MiniMax M3.1 Flash today, and Tenstorrent is now serving it on Cloud, with both prefill and decode running on Tenstorrent Galaxy®.

MiniMax M3.1 Flash runs agent tasks at 70% lower cost than M3, with strong results on coding, computer use, and cybersecurity.

Benchmark results published by MiniMax.

MiniMax M3.1 Flash is built to run agents in production:

- Lower cost per token vs M3: $0.15 per 1M input tokens, $0.60 per 1M output tokens, and $0.015 per 1M cached input tokens; 50% of M3’s price for input and output, and 25% for cached input.
- Strong benchmarks: Tops every model in MiniMax’s comparison on AutomationBench (62.8) and LOCA-Bench 256K (60.3), and ties Claude Opus 5 on BankerToolBench (76.2).
- Proven at scale: “Space Bunny Alpha,” the anonymous model that processed more than 200 trillion tokens, was an early version of MiniMax M3.1 Flash.

...

### How we serve MiniMax M3.1 Flash on Tenstorrent

We serve MiniMax M3.1 Flash on a supercluster of Tenstorrent Blackhole Galaxies, with Galaxies split by prefill and decode, so each system can be tuned for its own job:

- Prefill: processes agent prompts. High bandwidth between devices enables each prompt to spread across many chips without stalling on data movement.
- Decode: generates tokens on Galaxy systems independent of those used for prefill, so long prefills don’t stall users mid-response. Chips pass work along a pipeline over direct, low-latency Ethernet links. Weights and KV cache stay on-device in DRAM, while on-chip SRAM allows each step to execute fast.
- KV cache offload: keeps reused context close at hand. Each Blackhole Galaxy has 1 TB of DRAM and several terabytes of SSD, so context stays cached longer and returning agent turns do not recompute input they’ve already processed.

Tenstorrent tunes on SemiAnalysis’s AgentX coding-agent traces, captured from real multi-turn sessions and subagent fan-out, rather than short chat benchmarks.

- Ground: give agents trusted meaning for metrics, entities and relationships.

signals.title: How we fit a 27B model on a 12 GB laptop GPU - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
How we fit a 27B model on a 12 GB laptop GPU - DEV Community
Posted on Nov 1 • Originally published at genrius-ai.github.io
# How we fit a 27B model on a 12 GB laptop GPU
## In short
* Qwen3.8-27B goes from 53.8 GB of 16-bit weights to an 8.31 GB Pingala-8 file, 84.5% smaller (6.5x). It runs with every layer on one 12 GB RTX 5070 Ti Laptop GPU at 37.7 tokens/s (llama-bench, batch 1).
* Version 2 moves bits between tensor roles and layer depths, following the allocation in DASH-Q's published files. WikiText-2 perplexity fell from 7.34 to 6.89 at the same size, better on 20 of 20 test windows.
* DASH-Q IQ2\_XS (8.55 GB) is still better than ours: 6.54, ahead on 20 of 20 windows. Against unsloth UD-IQ2\_S (8.37 GB, 7.34) our lower average is not a significant win.
* The file needs our patched llama.cpp runtime on an NVIDIA GPU. Stock llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio cannot load it.
## The problem: 53.8 GB of weights, 12 GB of memory
Qwen3.8-27B is a 27-billion-parameter model. Its text weights, stored the way the Qwen team ships them at 16 bits each, come to 53.8 GB. That count leaves out the vision tower and the multi-token-prediction block, which we do not ship either.
A model runs at full speed only when its weights sit in GPU memory, next to the cache that holds the conversation. A laptop GPU with 12 GB cannot hold 53.8 GB. Even at 4 bits per weight, the weights alone would be about 13.5 GB (a quarter of 53.8), more than the whole card before any cache. The usual answer is to leave some layers in system RAM, which slows generation to the speed of that slower memory.
We wanted the whole model on the GPU. That means about 2 bits per weight.
## What 2-bit means
A weight is one number in one of the model's matrices. At 16 bits it takes 2 bytes. At 2 bits it takes a quarter of a byte, so on its own it could take only 4 different values. No useful format stores weights that crudely. 2-bit formats code small groups of weights together, keep a scale for each block of weights, and store a few sensitive tensors with more bits. The "2-bit" label describes the bulk of the file, not every byte of it.
For our file the arithmetic is simple: 8.31 GB for 53.8 GB of 16-bit weights is 6.5x smaller, or about 2.5 bits per weight averaged over the whole file. The extra half bit pays for the scales, the token embedding and output head, and the tensors that get more than 2 bits.
Fewer bits means rounding error, and the error adds up across 27 billion weights. We measure what that costs with WikiText-2 perplexity, a standard score for how well a model predicts real text; lower is better. Our article on 8 models explains the score in plain words.
Pingala-8 codes each row of weights in groups of 4 with an 8-state trellis code, after a random Hadamard rotation and LDLQ rounding. These ideas come from QuIP, QuIP# and QTIP; the trellis-coded quantization guide explains them. This article is about something else: how many bits each tensor gets.
## The 8.31 GB file
The release is 8,314,241,600 bytes in 9 parts on Hugging Face. On our one test machine, an RTX 5070 Ti Laptop GPU with 12 GB under WSL2, it loads with every layer on the GPU (`-ngl 99`) and leaves room for a 4,096-token context. The 12 GB guide and the VRAM requirements page show the memory arithmetic for longer contexts and other cards. We have not run this file on any other GPU.
## The real-speed demo 
 Real run, real speed. Text and timing captured from the run; terminal view re-rendered. Chat speed in this run: 31.63 tokens/s (runtime eval, 124 tokens, thinking off); the 37.7 tokens/s above is llama-bench tg64. Watch the 1080p MP4.
The clip replays one chat run on that laptop: every token appears when it was captured, nothing is sped up, and only the terminal view is redrawn. It shows two speeds on purpose. 37.7 tokens/s is the llama-bench generation test. 31.63 tokens/s is the runtime's own count for this chat answer. They are different measurements, we have not yet looked into the gap, and we report both.
## What we changed in version 2: bits by role and depth
A transformer is a stack of layers, and each layer holds several kinds of matrix: the attention projections (`attn\_qkv` builds the queries, keys and values), the feed-forward matrices (`ffn\_up`, `ffn\_gate`, `ffn\_down`), and in Qwen3.8's linear-attention layers an output projection called `ssm\_out`. We call the kind of matrix its role, and its position in the stack its depth. A 2-bit file does not have to give every tensor the same number of bits. The question is where the extra bits do the most good.
Version 1 copied the layout llama.cpp uses for its IQ2\_XXS type. That layout spent 4.5 bits per weight on `attn\_qkv`, and the rest of the budget had to come from somewhere else.
DASH-Q, a set of 2-bit GGUF files published by jkim96, splits the budget differently. We read the type of every tensor out of their Qwen3.8-27B file and built the same plan for ours: a bit budget for each role in each band of layers, from early to late. Same total bytes, different placement; the change was the allocation, not the coding method.
The result, on the same 20 WikiText-2 windows:
* Version 1: perplexity 7.34.
* Version 2: perplexity 6.89, lower on all 20 windows, at the same 8.31 GB.
The allocation idea is DASH-Q's, not ours. What we added is the evidence that the same plan helps a different coder.
### The smaller model taught us the rest
We then tried to copy the 27B plan onto Qwen3.5-2B. It did not help: perplexity 15.80 against 15.62 for version 1, better on only 22 of 70 windows. The 27B plan spent too much on the late feed-forward layers (4.1 bits per weight) and starved `ssm\_out` (2.6) for a model of this size. A plan learned on one model is not a plan for every model.
The second gap was the embedding. In the 2B, the token embedding and the output head are the same matrix. DASH-Q stores it at Q4\_K, 286 MB. We stored it at Q5\_K, 350 MB. At equal file size, that left DASH-Q 489 MB for the other matrices against our 429 MB, 14% more.
So the third try moved the embedding to Q4\_K, which freed 61.6 MB, and used DASH-Q's own 2B plan for the rest. That file scored 14.06 at 778,189,408 bytes, slightly smaller than version 1 and better on 70 of 70 windows, a 10.0% drop in perplexity. It is now version 2 of our Qwen3.5-2B. The lesson we wrote down: the embedding and output head are part of the byte budget, so copy the leading file's whole-file allocation, not just its large matrices.
## What failed: water-filling
We also tried to derive an allocation ourselves instead of copying one. Water-filling is the textbook answer from rate-distortion theory: measure how much error each tensor suffers at each bit rate, then hand out bits where they cut the most error, until every tensor gains the same from one more bit. We used a per-tensor error measure from our encoder.
We tested it where tests are cheap, on Qwen3.5-0.8B, at about 35 minutes of GPU time in all: \*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*
|Qwen3.5-0.8B plan|Perplexity|vs DASH-Q plan|
|DASH-Q role and depth plan|23.72|reference|
|Water-filling, variant 1|26.72|+0.120 nats/token|
|Water-filling, variant 2|25.71|+0.081 nats/token|
WikiText-2, lower is better. The last column is the paired per-window loss difference; positive means worse than the DASH-Q plan.
Both variants lost clearly, so we stopped and logged the result. We do not know exactly why. One plausible reason is that the error of a tensor measured on its own is a poor guide to what the whole model loses when that tensor gets fewer bits. Either way, the DASH-Q plan won, and that is the one we shipped.
## The honest comparison
Here are the five Qwen3.8-27B files we measured on the same text, the same 20 windows and the same laptop. Lower is better. \*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*
|2-bit file|Size|PPL|Against ours (v2)|
|DASH-Q IQ2\_XS|8.55 GB|6.54|Better than ours on 20/20 windows|
|Pingala-8 v2 (ours)|8.31 GB|6.89||
|unsloth UD-IQ2\_S|8.37 GB|7.34|Ours lower on average; not significant (9/20)|
|Pingala-8 v1 (ours)|8.31 GB|7.34|v2 better on 20/20|
|llama.cpp IQ2\_XXS, same imatrix|8.43 GB|7.88|Ours lower|
WikiText-2 test, 4,096-token windows, the first 20 windows for every file. Every window is in the eval dataset and ranked on the 2-bit GGUF leaderboard.
DASH-Q is better. Its lead over us is 0.052 nats per token, with a 95% interval of plus or minus 0.012, and it holds on every window. That is about 5% in perplexity, for 0.24 GB more file.
The unsloth comparison is the opposite case. Our average is lower, 6.89 against 7.34, but we are better on only 9 of 20 windows, and the paired interval (-0.064 plus or minus 0.075) includes zero. We do not count that as a win. Our benchmarking article explains the paired test and why a lower average is not enough.
We did not compare speed with the rival files. On our GPU their IQ1\_S, IQ2\_S and IQ3\_S tensors had to run on the CPU (the NaN page explains why), so a speed number from our machine would be unfair to them. Both rival files use standard llama.cpp types and load in stock llama.cpp; ours does not.
So when is ours the right file? When you run our runtime on an NVIDIA card and want the smallest of the files that fit, and one measured fully on the GPU. If quality comes first, or you want stock llama.cpp, Ollama or LM Studio, take DASH-Q.
## How to run it
Build llama.cpp at commit `7ac59a6` with the Pingala-8 CUDA patch and the Qwen3.5 loader change, then download the 9 parts and pass part 1:
```
git clone https://github.com/Genrius-AI/pingala8-llm
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp
git checkout 7ac59a6e3ad851cd41af00f678effab0598ba9a8
git apply ../pingala8-llm/patches/llama_cuda_vs_7ac59a6.patch
git apply ../pingala8-llm/patches/q35_loader_count_delta.patch
cmake -S . -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DLLAMA_OPENSSL=OFF
cmake --build build -j8 --target llama-cli llama-perplexity llama-bench

# Introducing AgentEnv: An Open-Source Framework for Building RL Environments

By Edgar Arakelyan, Tejas Polakam, Yzabelle Go

An agent is only as good as the world it operates in, and building worlds that are realistic, accurate, and scalable all at once is the hard part of scaling RL. Every RL environment Scale builds runs on AgentEnv. Today we're open-sourcing it.

...

Building blocks: What an Environment is made of. An Environment is built from versioned composable blocks: Environments like Slack or Gmail, an Artifact of data that populates them, and Rules (the clock, triggers, and roles) that govern how it behaves.

Interoperability: What an Environment works with. An Environment doesn't assume anything about who or what runs it. Any agent can connect to it, any sandbox can host it, and your cloud can run it, all through open protocols instead of custom glue.

...

Agent Agnostic. An Environment's card tells an agent which tools it serves and how to reach them, over MCP, REST or a generated CLI. An agent's Agent Card, from the open A2A protocol, does the same in the other direction.

Pair any Environment Card with any Agent Card and the agent can start work, with no custom wiring. The same Task runs unchanged and consistent on Claude Code, OpenAI's agents, or any of your own custom agents.

...

A Task is constructed as a DAG of AgentEnv steps. Each step represents a primitive action on an Agent, the Environment and more, like setting up the world, loading data, setting the clock, bringing in an agent, handing it the work, collecting what it made, grading the result with a rubric or a strict check.

...

AgentEnv ships 48 built-in step types, covering everything from deploying an Environment to setting its Rules of the World to grading trajectories. Most RL Tasks can be built from these alone, with no new code. For the rest, you can add your own steps as plugins.

signals.title: DeepSeek Open-Sources Super-agent Architecture: Breaking Through the Single-Session Agent Bottleneck with Classic Computer System Ideas
signals.excerpt:
On the evening of October 31, the DeepSeek Harness team officially announced the underlying architecture for its exploration of autonomous agents—Super-agent (superintelligent agent)—and open-sourced it on GitHub.

This achievement is not a standalone new product. Instead, it introduces classic ideas from computer systems—such as scheduling, caching, storage-compute separation, and watchdog—into the agent architecture, attempting to take over session management and context synchronization at the underlying layer. In doing so, it aims to free up human attention and drive the agent application experience from a passive chat window toward an always-on autonomous collaborator.

Faced with the limitations of traditional single-session agents in multi-task concurrency, context confusion, and human intervention, the core architecture of Super-agent consists of five major modules. In its two-layer architecture, the system is split into a resident Router layer (responsible for unified routing and external interaction) and an isolated, concurrent Worker layer (focused on executing specific tasks), effectively balancing global continuity and high-concurrency throughput.

...

Preliminary experimental data show that the Super-agent based on this approach performs excellently in task completion efficiency: half of the tasks can be completed within 12.4 minutes, and 95% of tasks within 15.7 minutes, significantly outperforming traditional single-session solutions.

Meanwhile, the subscription pass-through mechanism saves the Router layer about 37% of Token overhead, while the batching mechanism reduces the amortized inference time per decision from 6.4 seconds to 1.6 seconds. Although the current experiments are based on a simplified environment and still face challenges such as two-layer scaling and security and privacy, this architecture preliminarily proves the feasibility of having the system layer take over session scheduling, providing an important industry reference for balancing efficiency and stability in multi-task agents.

signals.title: Mistral Releases 1-Trillion-Parameter AI Model for Cybersecurity
signals.excerpt:
Mistral AI is giving security teams another option for running advanced AI models without relying entirely on outside cloud providers.

The French artificial intelligence developer publicly released the weights for its 1-trillion-parameter flagship model, Mistral Large 4, on Oct. 29. The move lets public agencies and private enterprises download, inspect, and host the software directly on their own hardware.

Following a three-week public preview, Mistral added focused reinforcement learning to tune the system for autonomous software development and vulnerability management, positioning it as an open rival to closed systems from OpenAI and Google.

...

Mistral Large 4 scored 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, reflecting an ability to locate software bugs, reproduce them in sandboxes, and patch source code without breaking features.

The company noted that the model blocks malicious requests with a 96.6% refusal rate while remaining accessible to security analysts performing legitimate administrative audits.

In software engineering benchmarks, the model reached 41% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, edging out China’s open-weight GLM-5.3. On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 tied GLM-5.3 with a 48% score while consuming 47% fewer computational tokens per task.

...

The weights are available immediately on Hugging Face, alongside cloud access through Mistral’s commercial API, NVIDIA NIM containers, and Microsoft Foundry. Mistral lists API pricing at $0.70 per million input tokens and $2.10 per million output tokens, with cached input costing $0.07 per million tokens.

Before deploying Mistral Large 4, IT teams should assess whether their infrastructure can support the model’s memory and computing requirements, along with the costs of hosting and maintaining it.

signals.title: Entire Launches Agent-First Git Platform With Evals — AI In Context
signals.excerpt:
Entire, the developer platform from former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, is live with agent-run evals, decentralized Git hosting, session memory and company speed claims.

...

Entire said: “Unlike the classic Pull Request model of reviewing code changes with a diff, Trails offer developers a heads-up display similar to an airline pilot, with customized evals that are scored by agents on every code push.”

Entire presents the proposed idea, the agent trace and the session outcome as first-class artifacts for review alongside the code. The design shifts the default task from inspecting a line-by-line diff to validating agent-generated evaluations before a merge. The quality of those evaluations now determines whether a human can approve code without reading every generated line.

Entire treats review as a feedback system. A push produces evaluations, agents address findings, the developer validates progress, and the merge follows once every evaluation passes.

Entire said: “All data is available not only on Entire’s web interface, but also through the open-source Entire CLI. This allows coding agents to address findings in a loop, while the human developer validates the progress. When all evals are satisfied, they can merge the code without needing to look at the code itself.”

The open-source Entire CLI gives agents access to findings they can address in a loop, while Entire’s web interface exposes the same data to developers. Under the company’s workflow, an agent works through failing findings, the developer validates the progress, and the code can merge once every evaluation passes. The model reduces manual diff review, but it also makes the agent’s evaluation process part of the merge gate.

...

Continuous Memory keeps developer session logs next to code in the repository and uses them as a data source. Coding agents can search those records for answers, and Entire says the approach helps them use up to 71% fewer tokens.

...

The launch combines Trails, decentralized hosting and Continuous Memory in a platform for developers working with AI-generated code.

candidates.topic: AMD vs NVIDIA for AI inference cost
candidates.angle: AMD MI355X delivers Kimi K3 inference at 2.3x lower cost ($0.077 vs $0.179 per million tokens) than NVIDIA B200 at 100 tokens/second/user due to larger HBM capacity and kernel tuning.
candidates.audience_pain: The high cost of AI inference hardware, especially for large models, makes hardware selection a critical financial decision.
candidates.why_now: New benchmarks provide competitive data for alternative hardware, challenging NVIDIA's market dominance in AI accelerators.
candidates.hook_seed: AMD cheaper for agent inference than NVIDIA?

candidates.angle: Vercel Labs' open-source `agent-desktop` CLI enables AI agents to control native macOS, Windows, and Linux applications by reading the operating system’s accessibility tree, providing JSON snapshots for interaction without the need for vision models.
candidates.audience_pain: AI agents often struggle with reliable interaction with graphical user interfaces (GUIs) and native desktop applications, limiting their automation capabilities.
candidates.why_now: As agents become more sophisticated, the ability to robustly interact with and control desktop environments becomes crucial for real-world tasks.
candidates.hook_seed: Open-source CLI for agent desktop control

candidates.angle: DeepSeek's Super-agent architecture applies classic computer system ideas like scheduling, caching, storage-compute separation, and watchdogs to overcome the single-session agent bottleneck, enabling robust multi-task concurrency and context synchronization.
candidates.audience_pain: Current AI agents struggle with multi-tasking, context management across sessions, and maintaining state, limiting their utility in complex workflows.
candidates.why_now: As AI agents become more capable, the architectural challenges of making them robust and autonomous in complex environments are coming to the forefront.

candidates.angle: The `agentic-rag-faithfulness` library evaluates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) faithfulness locally in under 1 millisecond, avoiding expensive LLM judges and supporting both English and Arabic to detect LLM hallucinations efficiently.
candidates.audience_pain: Evaluating RAG system faithfulness is often slow and costly, relying on expensive LLM judges and adding significant latency to development cycles.
candidates.why_now: As RAG systems become more prevalent, the need for fast, local, and cost-effective evaluation tools is critical for rapid iteration and deployment.

candidates.angle: qwenGPU is an experimental model that compiles a SIMT GPU directly into the weights of Qwen3.5-2B, allowing real CUDA code, compiled to NVIDIA PTX, to run within its own forward passes for exact computation inside an LLM.
candidates.audience_pain: LLMs struggle with exact computation, requiring external tools. Embedding computation directly could revolutionize model capabilities.
candidates.why_now: This novel approach challenges current assumptions about model architecture and how LLMs perform computations, sparking new research directions.

candidates.angle: NVIDIA's optimizations for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model inference, including Humming MXFP4 kernels and online FP8 quantization, significantly reduce decode time from 27.71 ms to 9.72 ms by addressing memory-bound bottlenecks.
candidates.audience_pain: High latency and memory requirements make deploying Mixture-of-Experts models costly and slow for real-time applications.
candidates.why_now: New techniques are being published to make MoE models more practical for inference, a critical step for their wider adoption.

candidates.angle: Integrating AI tools or agents into development workflows can incur significant 'AI costs' due to the computational overhead of popular JavaScript frameworks, impacting performance and efficiency.
candidates.audience_pain: Developers face unexpected performance bottlenecks or higher compute costs when trying to integrate AI into existing web applications built with common JavaScript frameworks.
candidates.why_now: The increasing push to integrate AI features into web apps highlights overlooked compatibility and performance challenges.
candidates.hook_seed: Your JS framework costs AI performance

candidates.angle: NVIDIA TensorRT, combined with FP8 quantization, dramatically accelerates Stable Diffusion 3.5 on RTX GPUs, doubling performance (2.3x speedup) and reducing VRAM usage by 40%.
candidates.audience_pain: Slow image generation and high VRAM usage on local GPUs hinder creative workflows and accessibility for developers.
candidates.why_now: Ongoing optimizations continue to push the performance boundaries for popular generative AI models on consumer hardware.
